questions.title: Does §1216 independently require OSC to investigate FOIA violations, or does §552(a)(4)(F)(i) limit OSC's investigative authority?
questions.question_body: The district court held that §552(a)(4)(F)(i) does not limit OSC's power to investigate FOIA violations under §1216, meaning OSC's refusal to investigate was based on a legal error. But the D.C. Circuit never reached this merits question because it dismissed on standing grounds. I'm confused about the relationship between these two provisions. §1216(a)(3) says OSC "shall conduct an investigation" of arbitrary FOIA withholdings, while §552(a)(4)(F)(i) requires OSC to initiate disciplinary proceedings only after a court has (1) ordered production of records, (2) awarded attorneys' fees, and (3) specifically questioned whether the agency acted arbitrarily or capriciously. Do these provisions create independent obligations, or does the FOIA provision function as a limitation on the broader §1216 duty? Does it matter that one is in the Civil Service Reform Act and the other in FOIA itself?

questions.title: What is a 'procedural right in vacuo' and how does it interact with relaxed standing for procedural injuries?
questions.question_body: The court says the deprivation of a procedural right "in vacuo" is insufficient for standing (citing Summers v. Earth Island Institute). But it also discusses "relaxed standing requirements" for procedural injuries (citing Ctr. for Law & Educ. v. Dep't of Educ.), under which imminence and redressability are relaxed but injury in fact and causation are not. I'm confused about how these concepts fit together. If AFL has a procedural right to an OSC investigation under §1216, why doesn't the violation of that right itself constitute an injury in fact? What is the "concrete interest" that must be affected by the procedural deprivation, and why wasn't AFL's interest in the FOIA records or in the investigation's fruits sufficient?

questions.title: How attenuated is too attenuated for traceability when an injury requires a chain of actions by multiple non-party agencies?
questions.question_body: The court rejects AFL's first standing theory because the causal chain from OSC's refusal to investigate to AFL not receiving FOIA records is too speculative. The chain requires: (1) OSC investigates, (2) OSC decides to pursue corrective or disciplinary action, (3) MSPB decides to sanction DOJ employees, and (4) DOJ decides to produce records. MSPB and DOJ are not parties to the lawsuit. The court cites FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine for the rule that causation can't rely on "unfettered choices made by independent actors not before the courts." But many standing cases involve indirect causation through third parties. Where is the line between acceptable indirect causation and impermissibly speculative chains? Does the number of links matter, or is it about the nature of each link—e.g., whether each step is mandatory vs. discretionary?

questions.title: What makes information 'entitled' under a statute for purposes of informational injury standing?
questions.question_body: The court rejects AFL's second standing theory because, even if §1216 requires OSC to investigate, it "creates no entitlement to receive information." AFL argued that if OSC investigated under §1216, it might provide the notices and information required under §1214. But the court notes that §1214's notice requirements are discretionary when applied to §1216 investigations (citing Carson v. U.S. Office of Special Counsel). I'm confused about what distinguishes a statutory "entitlement" to information from mere potential access. In FEC v. Akins and Pub. Citizen v. DOJ, plaintiffs had statutory rights to receive information. What specific statutory language or structure creates an "entitlement"? Is it purely about mandatory vs. discretionary disclosure, or is there more to it?

questions.title: Why does redressability fail when ordering the defendant to do what the statute says it 'shall' do?
questions.question_body: The court says a favorable judgment wouldn't likely redress AFL's injuries because redressability "turns on how a judgment binds the parties, not whether its rationale might persuade actors who are not before the court" (citing Haaland v. Brackeen). But if the court orders OSC to conduct the investigation that §1216 says it "shall" conduct, isn't OSC bound by that order? Even if MSPB and DOJ aren't parties, the OSC investigation could lead to corrective action against DOJ employees. Why is the connection between an OSC investigation and eventual FOIA disclosure too remote for redressability? Is the court saying that even mandatory agency actions can't redress injuries if the ultimate relief depends on subsequent decisions by non-party actors?

questions.title: How does Heckler v. Chaney's presumption against judicial review of agency enforcement apply when a statute uses mandatory 'shall' language?
questions.question_body: The court cites Heckler v. Chaney for the proposition that courts generally may not compel agencies to exercise enforcement discretion, and uses this to support its causation analysis. But §1216 says OSC "shall conduct an investigation" of alleged FOIA violations. Doesn't mandatory statutory language override the Heckler presumption? Under the APA, agency action "committed to agency discretion by law" is unreviewable, but doesn't mandatory "shall" language create a clear standard for review that takes the matter out of the Heckler presumption? The court seems to treat OSC's decision about whether to pursue corrective or disciplinary action after investigating as discretionary, but what about the initial investigation itself—is that also discretionary despite the "shall" language?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the district court's judgment rather than simply reversing it?
questions.question_body: The D.C. Circuit "vacate[s] the district court's judgment and remand[s] with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction." The district court reached the merits and dismissed AFL's claims for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6). The D.C. Circuit found a jurisdictional defect (lack of Article III standing). Why vacatur rather than just reversal? Is this because the district court never should have reached the merits without first establishing jurisdiction, per Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment? And what's the practical difference for AFL between a dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under Rule 12(b)(1) and a dismissal for failure to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6)—can AFL refile either way, or is the jurisdictional dismissal more final?
